title: Proxy: Multi-hop Proxy
summary: Multi-hop proxying chains two or more relays so that command and control traffic leaves the victim through several intermediate hosts before reaching adversary infrastructure. Typical implementations include onion routing networks such as Tor, where traffic is wrapped in layered encryption and forwarded by relays that each know only the previous and next hop, and operational relay box networks built from rented virtual private servers, Internet of Things devices, smart appliances and end-of-life routers. Relays may also be compromised routers or other network devices running modified firmware, with tunnels carried inside protocols such as ICMP, or peer-to-peer and blockchain overlays. From the defender's view the flow usually terminates at one visible hop only, so the upstream source stays hidden. Detection is therefore best treated as anomaly hunting on egress behaviour: long-lived encrypted sessions to hosting or proxy providers, uniform packet sizes and timing, connections to addresses with no business relationship, and self-signed or mismatched certificates. Comparing destination reputation and connection regularity against a baseline of normal business traffic separates a relay chain from ordinary cloud use.

beginner.definition: A multi-hop proxy is a chain of computers that pass your network traffic from one to the next, hiding where it really started. Each computer in the chain only knows the one before it and the one after it. This technique is a sub-technique of Proxy, which is the general idea of hiding the true source of traffic.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers use these chains so that defenders cannot trace stolen data back to them. If you only watch the last relay, you will see an innocent company or router and stop there. This makes takedown, blocking and legal action much harder. It also means the first alert you see is often only one small part of a much longer path.
howItWorks: The attacker builds or rents several relay hosts in different networks and countries.
Malware on the victim sends traffic to the first relay only, wrapped in encryption.
That relay cannot read the data; it only forwards it to the next relay in the list.
Each relay removes one layer of wrapping, like opening nested envelopes one at a time.
The final relay delivers the traffic to the real control server that answers the malware.
In onion networks the relays are volunteers, so the owner never has to rent any of them.
beginner.example: Think of a chain of neighbours passing a sealed letter. You give an envelope to your neighbour, who cannot read it. That neighbour puts it in another envelope and passes it to a friend, who does the same again. Only the last person in the chain opens everything and reads the message. If you ask the last person who sent it, they can only name the neighbour before them. To find you, someone would have to ask every single person in the chain, and some of them live in other countries.
takeaways: You usually see only the last hop, so a clean-looking source may still be a relay.
Watch for long encrypted sessions to hosting providers that are not part of normal business traffic.
Hunt for beacon-like timing and regular packet sizes rather than for a known bad address.

objectives: Describe how a multi-hop proxy chain hides the original source of command and control traffic.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent Proxy technique and from a single relay.
Identify the network artefacts, including long-lived encrypted sessions and beacon regularity, that a relay chain leaves in logs.
Distinguish relay or hosting provider traffic from legitimate cloud and business traffic during triage.
List the log sources, such as firewall, proxy and network flow records, that support this investigation.
